questions.question: Name the economically marginalised groups, attach the mechanism of exclusion to each, and explain why removing the discriminatory laws did not remove their results.
questions.expected_answer: Black South Africans — stripped of land ownership by statute, confined in residence and trade, given deliberately inferior schooling, funnelled into low-wage migrant labour. Women, especially Black women — barred by law and custom from property, contracts and credit, carrying unpaid care work that limits hours available for paid work, still clustered in the lowest-paid occupations. Rural communities — settled in areas with the least infrastructure, thinnest markets and longest distances from employment. People with disabilities — inaccessible schools, transport and workplaces plus persistent employer assumptions. Youth — the newest entrants to a labour market with too few openings, inheriting earlier exclusions as their starting position. The categories intersect and compound. Removing the laws did not remove the results because economic position is inherited: the unowned house still provides no collateral, the denied trade cannot be taught to the next generation, and the distant address remains distant — so equal laws can coexist with a deeply unequal economy.

questions.question: Organise redress through the four factors of production. For each factor state what was denied, the instrument that answers it, and the support the instrument needs.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources/land — dispossession answered by restitution (return or compensation for post-1913 dispossession), redistribution (access for those never permitted to own) and tenure reform (securing insecure occupation); needs finance, equipment, training and market access, or the transfer produces no livelihood. Labour — denial of better jobs and the schooling behind them answered by employment equity, targeting management and professional levels where exclusion bit hardest, and levy-funded skills development through learnerships, apprenticeships and artisan training. Capital — exclusion from asset ownership and credit answered by B-BBEE ownership stakes, management representation, enterprise and supplier development and preferential procurement, plus development finance for borrowers without collateral. Entrepreneurship — restricted business rights answered by incubation, mentorship, simplified compliance for small firms and procurement set-asides that provide a first customer. The refrain: every instrument needs its support conditions, and the test is whether a programme hands over an object or leaves a working livelihood.

questions.question: Describe how economic decision-making has been democratised, and evaluate redress with both ledgers open.
questions.expected_answer: Democratisation: labour legislation gives workers the rights to organise, bargain and be consulted, making them parties to decisions; public participation requires parliamentary submissions, municipal consultation on development plans and regulatory hearings before tariff or licence decisions; NEDLAC seats government, organised business, organised labour and organised community, negotiating major labour legislation and economic policy before Parliament through consensus-seeking social dialogue — durable buy-in, but slow, and weakly organised constituencies are heard least; self-regulating professional and industry bodies enforce their own codes inside a legal framework with public accountability. Evaluation: achievements — millions connected to water, electricity and housing, grants holding back destitution, a large Black professional and middle class, shifted ownership and management, new rights and institutions. Shortfalls — unemployment persistently extreme, income and wealth inequality among the world's worst, land reform behind its targets and often unsupported after transfer, and benefits sometimes pooled among a connected few, the critique that produced 'broad-based'. Both columns must be stated with mechanisms, keeping evidence separate from preference.
